lessons: Start with vivid, relatable visual comparisons (e.g., cars stacked on teeth or baby size like a small dog) to secure high 10% retention (1.02 to 1.05+).
Avoid immediate repetition or redundant restatements of the hook within the primary drop windows (around 10-25% progress), as this triggers high drop-off rates.
Do not include countdowns or slow, overly complex theoretical explanations mid-video, as data shows significant viewer loss during dense exposition phases.
Keep early exposition concise and grounded in direct narrative progression; prolonged setup around 12% to 25% consistently results in double-digit audience loss.
Sustain high comparative performance at the end by delivering high-stakes reveals or payoff questions before the 50% mark, driving better relative retention versus benchmark videos.
worst_moment_types: Dense scientific explanations or heavy technical detailing (e.g., bone-by-bone computer reconstructions, exact newton force metrics) without immediate payoff
Repeated phrasing or cyclical explanations that re-state the hook premise instead of advancing the narrative
Mid-video transition zones (12% to 30% mark) where pacing slows down before delivering the core conflict or answer
best_hook_types: Extreme hypothetical scenarios involving everyday objects (e.g., T. rex speed compared to a car, car crash physics)
Direct personal framing ('Imagine you are a baby T. rex...') that instantly places the viewer in the narrative
Challenging common pop-culture myths right at the opening sentence
